transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-10
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Monroe (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Redwood SE), Sam Torres (ACME CTO), Maya Patel (ACME Cloud Eng), Ravi Singh (ACME Security), Elena Gomez (PM)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect): Discovery on private VPC deployment, network connectivity options discussed.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood Inference. Quick intros?
[00:10] Sam: Sam Torres, CTO at ACME Energy. We're evaluating options to run inference on customer data, and privacy is key.
[00:18] Maya: Maya, cloud eng, I'll own network config.
[00:21] Ravi: Ravi, security, focusing on KMS, audit logs, and compliance.
[00:26] Alex: Great. Priya's our SE, she'll run through network patterns and options, Jordan's here too for any perf questions.
[00:33] Priya: Hi all. Quick agenda: we want to understand your constraints (regions, VPC setup, whether you want peering or private endpoints), then we'll map the architecture options - Redwood Hosted, Redwood Dedicated, Private (VPC) and tradeoffs.
[00:47] Elena: We have a regulatory requirement that no customer data leaves our VPC in the eu-west-1 region, ideally. Also key management has to be customer-controlled.
[00:58] Priya: Got it. So two high level options: 1) Dedicated – reserved GPU pool in our infra but still managed, or 2) Private deployment – private control plane and private endpoints, where the inference nodes sit in your VPC or connected VPCs. Hosted public API is probably off the table for the constraint you described.
[01:15] Sam: Right, hosted is a no. We want either private or dedicated with VPC isolation.
[01:21] Maya: A couple of specifics: we use AWS and we have transit gateway connecting multiple accounts. We prefer not to open wide internet egress. Would you support VPC peering or do you require PrivateLink / interface endpoints?
[01:33] Priya: We support multiple connectivity patterns. For AWS we commonly offer three: VPC peering (cross-account), AWS PrivateLink (interface VPC endpoints), and a private control plane option where Redwood's control plane sits in a private management VPC and nodes are in your account. Each has tradeoffs.
[01:47] Ravi: Security-wise, we favor PrivateLink because it avoids route table changes and you can restrict access with endpoint policies. But we also need to know about IP ranges and how many ENIs are created.
[01:57] Priya: Yes. With PrivateLink, you get an endpoint service on our side and you create interface endpoints in your subnets. That creates ENIs in your subnets and all traffic stays on the AWS backbone. We'll provide the endpoint DNS names and the exact ports (mostly 443/TLS). For peering, you'd have route table entries and you need to ensure no overlapping CIDRs. Peering is generally simpler but requires route management.
[02:18] Jordan: Just to add, for throughput-sensitive workloads, peering can have slightly lower latency vs PrivateLink in some cases because there's fewer network hops, but PrivateLink gives stronger isolation and policy control. Depends on your latency SLOs.
[02:33] Maya: Our primary region is eu-west-1 and we replicate for DR in eu-central-1. Do you provision in those regions?
[02:41] Priya: We have Dedicated and Private options in eu-west-1 today, and eu-central-1 availability is on the roadmap; for strict data residency you'd want nodes in the same region. If you need immediate multi-region, we can design a cross-region setup but with added complexity and potential egress. I'll flag that as a design item.
[02:58] Sam: We need KMS integration — customer-managed keys and an HSM-backed option.
[03:04] Priya: We support KMS integration. For Private deployments, you can bring your own KMS (AWS KMS) and we can integrate so that model artifacts and any stored cache can be encrypted with your keys. HSM is an add-on — we can discuss options, sometimes via dedicated hardware or partner HSMs. We'll include the integration notes in the docs.
[03:21] Ravi: Audit logs and retained telemetry — we need immutable audit logs for access and model inference events stored for 12 months. Also SSO; we use SAML SSO with SCIM provisioning.
[03:33] Alex: We have audit logging and can ship logs to your CloudWatch/Stackdriver/Splunk via a private log-forwarder. For SSO we support SAML and SCIM for user provisioning, RBAC is configurable.
[03:46] Elena: On the data plane, do you ever cache inputs or prompts outside our VPC? We're worried about exposure.
[03:53] Priya: By default Private deployment keeps the data plane within your VPC. We can disable external caching. For Hosted/Dedicated we have optional prefix/KV caching to reduce cost, but for strict privacy we can turn that off or ensure it uses encrypted customer-managed keys. We'll document defaults and how to opt out.
[04:12] Maya: Networking nit: what about egress NAT? We want to avoid giving nodes public IPs.
[04:18] Priya: You won't need public IPs. Nodes can be in private subnets behind NAT or use private endpoints to pull images from ECR via VPC endpoints. We recommend using interface endpoints for ECR, S3 gateway endpoints or a VPC endpoint to S3 to avoid public egress when pulling models.
[04:34] Ravi: How about region constraints for control plane? If the control plane is outside EU, is metadata ever sent there?
[04:42] Priya: For Private control plane deployments, the control plane can be deployed into a private management VPC in the same region to satisfy residency. For Dedicated we can provide region-isolated control plane options. We'll confirm the exact metadata flows in the architecture docs — short answer: we can keep control plane in-region and limit metadata leaving your region for the strictest scenario.
[05:03] Sam: What about provisioning times — how long to spin up a private deployment?
[05:08] Jordan: Typical timeline is a week for a test environment (assuming network prep), 2-4 weeks for production depending on approvals and sizing. Dedicated capacity lead times depend on reserved GPU availability.
[05:22] Elena: Cost — ballpark? We need apples-to-apples for Dedicated vs Private.
[05:27] Alex: We'll send a baseline pricing for a 3-node GPU cluster with expected throughput. Dedicated is typically lower per-token but requires commitment; Private has additional setup/ops and potential infra costs if nodes are in your account. We'll include an itemized cost comparison.
[05:43] Maya: Can you walk through firewall rules? What CIDRs do we need to allow?
[05:48] Priya: We'll provide a network guide with IP ranges (or endpoint DNS) and ports. For PrivateLink it's port 443 to endpoint ENIs. For peering it's all internal IPs — we'll give subnets and recommended route table entries. We'll also provide sample security group rules and WAF suggestions.
[06:07] Ravi: Do you support Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) for model weights and logs? How is key rotation handled?
[06:15] Priya: Yes BYOK for AWS KMS is supported. For rotation we can integrate with AWS KMS rotation policies; the service will use the current key for new items and we can help run a re-encryption operation if you need to rotate historical objects. We'll detail the process in the security notes.
[06:33] Sam: Regarding dependencies, do you require outbound access to our monitoring endpoints? We have strict egress rules.
[06:40] Alex: We can ship logs via your log endpoints over a private connection or via a log-forwarder in your VPC that pulls logs locally. We don't need general outbound internet if you prefer closed egress.
[06:52] Maya: How do you handle IP allowlists for admin access? We want to restrict console access and API access to our bastion IPs only.
[06:59] Priya: For Private deployments, we can restrict admin console and API access to your IP ranges via network policies and SAML SSO. For Dedicated, we have options to restrict by VPC or by IP. We'll include admin access-config steps in the runbook.
[07:14] Elena: Any gotchas re: overlapping CIDRs with third-party services?
[07:18] Priya: Overlapping CIDRs will block peering; if you have overlaps we usually recommend using PrivateLink or setting up a transit gateway with NAT and route translation. We'll walk through your current CIDR plan on the next call.
[07:30] Jordan: From a perf standpoint, what's the latency SLO you need?
[07:34] Sam: For front-end customer flows we need sub-200ms 95th for single-shot generation at 512 tokens, ideally under 100ms for short prompts.
[07:44] Jordan: Sub-200ms is achievable with co-located nodes and aggressive batching tuned for latency. For Private deployments in your region we'll get the lowest latency; Dedicated in-region is similar. If you need <100ms consistently, we'll need to benchmark with your workload.
[07:58] Maya: Benchmarking — can we run a pilot?
[08:01] Priya: Yes, we usually do a pilot with a small cluster and synthetic + real prompts. We'll need sample prompts, token lengths, and concurrency targets. We can run an initial perf sweep and share metrics.
[08:12] Sam: Also curious about model updates and version pinning. We need the ability to pin model versions and have rollbacks.
[08:19] Alex: You can pin model versions per route, do canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automatic fallbacks to compatible variants. We'll capture rollout policies in the runbook.
[08:30] Ravi: Compliance — we need to see SOC2 report and any penetration test summaries.
[08:35] Alex: We'll attach SOC2 and penetration test summaries to the security packet we send.
[08:41] Maya: Network wise, what's the number of ENIs or IPs required per node? That impacts our subnet sizing.
[08:48] Priya: Typically one or two ENIs per node for interface endpoints plus ENIs for PrivateLink. We'll provide exact numbers per instance type. For large clusters we'll give a recommended subnet sizing table.
[09:03] Elena: For the control plane, is there an operator in our account or do you maintain it?
[09:08] Priya: For Private deployments we can offer two modes: 1) Customer-managed data plane where nodes run in your account and Redwood provides the control plane in a private management VPC (we can also co-locate it in your account for the strictest model), or 2) Fully self-hosted on-prem package. We'll plan the architecture per your preference.
[09:27] Sam: We'd prefer the control plane in our account or in-region private management VPC to satisfy auditors.
[09:33] Alex: Noted. We'll note that as a hard requirement.
[09:36] Maya: Are there any surprises on logging costs or S3 egress when storing inference logs?
[09:42] Priya: If logs are stored in your S3 using VPC endpoints, costs are just your S3 storage. If we store logs in our account and ship copies to you, there may be egress or storage costs; we'll outline both models.
[09:56] Ravi: Is there a maximum model size you support in Private? We might want to run a 70B model.
[10:02] Jordan: We support a range of model sizes; for 70B you typically need model parallelism and appropriate GPU instances. We'll capture recommended instance types and quantization options; quantized variants reduce memory but can affect latency/quality tradeoffs.
[10:20] Maya: How do you handle kernel/compilation selection? I know some runtimes require specific CUDA versions.
[10:27] Jordan: Our runtime does kernel selection and is GPU-optimized. For Private deployments we'll match the instance type and CUDA/cuDNN versions — we'll include a compatibility matrix.
[10:39] Sam: Ok recap: we need network doc, SOC2 + security docs, KMS/HSM notes, pilot pricing, and a follow-up architecture session.
[10:48] Alex: Correct. I'll send the network guide and pricing. Priya will schedule the architecture deep dive. We'll include sample templates for VPC endpoints and recommended security group rules.
[10:59] Elena: One more question — how do you handle failover if a region goes down? Can we route to Dedicated in another region?
[11:07] Priya: Yes, we support fallbacks; the route is: if primary region nodes are unavailable we can route to a compatible model in a secondary region, but be mindful of data residency and potential egress. For critical regulatory constraints you may want synchronous replication in both regions. We'll discuss DR approaches next call.
[11:30] Sam: Sounds good.
[11:33] Alex: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and times.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription quality: Some names and product names may be slightly off (Redwood sometimes transcribed as Redwood Privatee or Redwood Infrence), timestamps approximate, a few words smoothed by the auto-transcriber.
